marble.name: Equivalent fractions
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators
marble.prompt: If you sees a bar divided into 4 equal parts with 2 shaded, can they tell you that's the same as 1/2 — and draw a different bar showing the same amount another way?

cluster.summary: Your child is discovering their first fractions — learning to recognise and name halves and quarters as equal parts of shapes, objects, and groups.

misconceptions: Whole-number bias — 4/6 judged more than 2/3 'because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces'
Different numbers must mean different amounts (denies equivalence)
Makes 'equivalents' by ADDING the same number to top and bottom (2/3 → 3/4)
Compares shaded amounts across different-sized wholes
Thinks changing only the numerator or only the denominator keeps the value
representations: Fraction wall / stacked equal-length bars (canonical equivalence reference)
A single bar re-partitioned by splitting each part (2/3 → 4/6)
Number line with dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) showing the same point
Area model (identical rectangles shaded to the same amount)
authoredAnswer: They are equal — 2/3 = 4/6. The same amount of chocolate is shaded on both bars; the second bar just has each third split into two, so four smaller sixths cover exactly the same length as two thirds. Mia is wrong: more pieces are each smaller, so the total amount is the same.
probe: Show the two fractions un-overlaid: a bar shaded 2/3 and an identical bar shaded 4/6, held apart. Ask the child to predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME amount as 2/3, and to say why before checking. A whole-number-biased child predicts '4/6 is more, because 4 > 2'. wrongAnswers.wrong: 4/6 is more, because 4 is more than 2 and it has more pieces.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says 4/6 is more chocolate and points to the larger numbers or the greater number of shaded pieces
wrongAnswers.fix: Overlay the two identical bars so the shaded lengths coincide; split each third to generate the sixths in front of the child so the amount is seen not to change

wrongAnswers.wrong: They must be different — the two fractions have different numbers.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Insists they must differ because the fractions are written with different numbers
wrongAnswers.fix: Show 2/3 and 4/6 landing on the same point on a number line and covering the same length on the wall; name both as one amount

wrongAnswers.wrong: 2/3 = 3/4 — I added one to the top and one to the bottom.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Generates an equivalent by +1 to each, or agrees 2/3 = 3/4
wrongAnswers.fix: Contrast +1-to-each (shifts the shaded strip) with split-each-part (leaves it fixed); establish that both parts must be MULTIPLIED

before.name: Finding halves and quarters (age 5+)
before.reason: the simplest equivalence (two quarters equal one half, seen in drawings) is the real readiness for small-denominator equivalence

before.name: Fractions on a number line
before.reason: Number line supports seeing equivalent fractions as the same point

before.name: Understanding fractions
before.reason: Showing equivalent fractions with diagrams does not require writing fraction-of-amount calculations (1/2 of 10 = 5); MyGb remains useful background. Real readiness is FbDK -> g3W0 (two quarters equal one half)

before.name: Fraction Notation
before.reason: Recognising and showing equivalent fractions requires that vocabulary

after.name: Equivalent fractions on a number line
